entries.content_plain:
CHAPTER 21
 
Ge 21:1-13. Birth of Isaac.

1. the Lord visited Sarah--The language of the historian seems designedly chosen to magnify the power of God as well as His faithfulness to His promise. It was God's grace that brought about that event, as well as the raising of spiritual children to Abraham, of which the birth of this son was typical [Calvin].

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv224"/><div sID="gen395" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv224"/><hi type="bold">3-4. Abraham called the name of his son ... Isaac ... and circumcised--</hi>God was acknowledged in the name which, by divine command, was given for a memorial (compare <reference osisRef="Gen.17.19">Ge 17:19</reference>), and also in the dedication of the child by administering the seal of the covenant (compare <reference osisRef="Gen.17.10-Gen.17.12">Ge 17:10-12</reference>). <div eID="gen395" type="x-p"/>
entries.content_plain: 3-4. Abraham called the name of his son ... Isaac ... and circumcised--God was acknowledged in the name which, by divine command, was given for a memorial (compare Ge 17:19), and also in the dedication of the child by administering the seal of the covenant (compare Ge 17:10-12).

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv225"/><div sID="gen396" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv225"/><hi type="bold">8. the child grew, and was weaned--</hi>children are suckled longer in the East than in the Occident--boys usually for two or three years.<div eID="gen396" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen397" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Abraham made a great feast, &c.--</hi>In Eastern countries this is always a season of domestic festivity, and the newly weaned child is formally brought, in presence of the assembled relatives and friends, to partake of some simple viands. Isaac, attired in the symbolic robe, the badge of birthright, was then admitted heir of the tribe [Rosenmuller]. <div eID="gen397" type="x-p"/>
entries.content_plain:
8. the child grew, and was weaned--children are suckled longer in the East than in the Occident--boys usually for two or three years.
 
Abraham made a great feast, &c.--In Eastern countries this is always a season of domestic festivity, and the newly weaned child is formally brought, in presence of the assembled relatives and friends, to partake of some simple viands. Isaac, attired in the symbolic robe, the badge of birthright, was then admitted heir of the tribe [Rosenmuller].

Sarah saw the son of Hagar ... mocking--</hi>Ishmael was aware of the great change in his prospects, and under the impulse of irritated or resentful feelings, in which he was probably joined by his mother, treated the young heir with derision and probably some violence (<reference osisRef="Gal.4.29">Ga 4:29</reference>). <div eID="gen398" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv227"/><div sID="gen399" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv227"/><hi type="bold">10. Wherefore she said unto Abraham, Cast out this bondwoman--</hi>Nothing but the expulsion of both could now preserve harmony in the household. Abraham's perplexity was relieved by an announcement of the divine will, which in everything, however painful to flesh and blood, all who fear God and are walking in His ways will, like him, promptly obey. This story, as the apostle tells us, in "an allegory" [Ga 4:24], and the "persecution" by the son of the Egyptian was the commencement of the four hundred years' affliction of Abraham's seed by the Egyptians. <div eID="gen399" type="x-p"/>

Abraham's perplexity was relieved by an announcement of the divine will, which in everything, however painful to flesh and blood, all who fear God and are walking in His ways will, like him, promptly obey. This story, as the apostle tells us, in "an allegory" [Ga 4:24], and the "persecution" by the son of the Egyptian was the commencement of the four hundred years' affliction of Abraham's seed by the Egyptians.

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv230"/><title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Gen.21.14-Gen.21.21">Ge 21:14-21</reference>. Expulsion of Ishmael.</title> <div sID="gen402" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv230"/><hi type="bold">14. Abraham rose up early, &c.--</hi>early, that the wanderers might reach an asylum before noon. Bread includes all sorts of victuals--bottle, a leathern vessel, formed of the entire skin of a lamb or kid sewed up, with the legs for handles, usually carried over the shoulder. Ishmael was a lad of seventeen years, and it is quite customary for Arab chiefs to send out their sons at such an age to do for themselves: often with nothing but a few days' provisions in a bag.<div eID="gen402" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen403" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">wandered in the wilderness of Beer-sheba--</hi>in the southern border of Palestine, but out of the common direction, a wide extending desert, where they lost their way. <div eID="gen403" type="x-p"/>
entries.content_plain:
Ge 21:14-21. Expulsion of Ishmael.

14. Abraham rose up early, &c.--early, that the wanderers might reach an asylum before noon. Bread includes all sorts of victuals--bottle, a leathern vessel, formed of the entire skin of a lamb or kid sewed up, with the legs for handles, usually carried over the shoulder. Ishmael was a lad of seventeen years, and it is quite customary for Arab chiefs to send out their sons at such an age to do for themselves: often with nothing but a few days' provisions in a bag.
 
wandered in the wilderness of Beer-sheba--in the southern border of Palestine, but out of the common direction, a wide extending desert, where they lost their way.

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv231"/><div sID="gen404" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv231"/><hi type="bold">15. the water was spent, &c.--</hi>Ishmael sank exhausted from fatigue and thirst--his mother laid his head under one of the bushes to smell the damp while she herself, unable to witness his distress, sat down at a little distance in hopeless sorrow. <div eID="gen404" type="x-p"/>
entries.content_plain: 15. the water was spent, &c.--Ishmael sank exhausted from fatigue and thirst--his mother laid his head under one of the bushes to smell the damp while she herself, unable to witness his distress, sat down at a little distance in hopeless sorrow.

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv232"/><div sID="gen405" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv232"/><hi type="bold">19. God opened her eyes--</hi>Had she forgotten the promise (<reference osisRef="Gen.16.11">Ge 16:11</reference>)? Whether she looked to God or not, He regarded her and directed her to a fountain close beside her, but probably hid amid brushwood, by the waters of which her almost expiring son was revived. <div eID="gen405" type="x-p"/>

God was with the lad, &c.--</hi>Paran (that is, Arabia), where his posterity has ever dwelt (compare <reference osisRef="Gen.16.12">Ge 16:12</reference>; also <reference osisRef="Isa.48.19">Is 48:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Pet.1.25">1Pe 1:25</reference>).<div eID="gen406" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen407" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">his mother took him a wife--</hi>On a father's death, the mother looks out for a wife for her son, however young; and as Ishmael was now virtually deprived of his father, his mother set about forming a marriage connection for him, it would seem, among her relatives. <div eID="gen407" type="x-p"/>
entries.content_plain:
20-21. God was with the lad, &c.--Paran (that is, Arabia), where his posterity has ever dwelt (compare Ge 16:12; also Is 48:19; 1Pe 1:25).
 
his mother took him a wife--On a father's death, the mother looks out for a wife for her son, however young; and as Ishmael was now virtually deprived of his father, his mother set about forming a marriage connection for him, it would seem, among her relatives.

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv234"/><title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Gen.21.22-Gen.21.34">Ge 21:22-34</reference>. Covenant.</title> <div sID="gen408" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv234"/><hi type="bold">22. Abimelech and Phichol--</hi>Here a proof of the promise (<reference osisRef="Gen.12.2">Ge 12:2</reference>) being fulfilled, in a native prince wishing to form a solemn league with Abraham. The proposal was reasonable, and agreed to [Ge 21:24]. <div eID="gen408" type="x-p"/>
entries.content_plain:
Ge 21:22-34. Covenant.

22. Abimelech and Phichol--Here a proof of the promise (Ge 12:2) being fulfilled, in a native prince wishing to form a solemn league with Abraham. The proposal was reasonable, and agreed to [Ge 21:24].

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv235"/><div sID="gen409" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv235"/><hi type="bold">25-31. And Abraham reproved Abimelech because of a well--</hi>Wells were of great importance to a pastoral chief and on the successful operation of sinking a new one, the owner was solemnly informed in person. If, however, they were allowed to get out of repair, the restorer acquired a right to them. In unoccupied lands the possession of wells gave a right of property in the land, and dread of this had caused the offense for which Abraham reproved Abimelech. Some describe four, others five, wells in Beer-sheba. <div eID="gen409" type="x-p"/>
